name: Takdah
tagline: An old army cantonment of bungalows, orchids and tea
meta_description: Takdah near Darjeeling: British-era cantonment bungalows, the orchid centre, Rungli Rungliot tea, the walk to Tinchuley, car fares and homestay prices.
summary: Takdah is a quiet former British army cantonment about 28 km from Darjeeling, at roughly 1,200–1,400 m above the Teesta valley. Old officers' bungalows, some now homestays, stand among tall pines, with a government orchid centre and the Rungli Rungliot and Gielle tea gardens close by. Expect ₹1,500–2,500 per person with meals.

local_story.title: A cantonment in the mist above the Teesta
paras: The local explanation of the name is Lepcha: tukdah, usually translated as mist, and anyone who has spent a July afternoon here will not argue. These slopes between Darjeeling and the Teesta were Lepcha and later Nepali farming country, part of the hill tract that passed from Sikkim into British hands in the middle of the nineteenth century. What changed Takdah was the army. In the early 1900s the British set up a cantonment on this spur, lower and milder than Darjeeling, and built a scatter of officers' bungalows among the trees, with wide verandahs, fireplaces and tin roofs.

The cantonment never grew into a town. Soldiers came and went, the bungalows outlasted the men they were built for, and the spur stayed a place of houses set far apart in their own gardens. Today some of those bungalows have been restored and opened to guests as heritage homestays, which is the main reason travellers find Takdah at all. Staying in one is not luxury: expect creaking wooden floors, high ceilings that take time to warm and a dining room where the family serves dal, local greens and chicken curry. It is, though, one of the cheaper ways in these hills to sleep in a house built for the Raj.

Two other stories run through Takdah. One is tea. The Rungli Rungliot garden lies on the slopes below, and the local story is that its name means 'thus far and no further'; ask in the village and you will hear it told. Gielle tea estate is close by too. The other story is flowers. The government orchid centre keeps nurseries of hill orchids, and from February to April its sheds are at their best. Between the tea and the orchids lives a village of farmers, garden workers and homestay families, with oranges ripening on the slopes in the winter sun.

did_you_know: Takdah was set up as a British army cantonment in the early 1900s, and several of its officers' bungalows still stand, some now let to guests as heritage homestays.
The local story is that Rungli Rungliot, the tea garden below Takdah, means 'thus far and no further'. Rangli Rangliot is also the name of a community development block of Darjeeling district.
Takdah lies about 28 km from Darjeeling but roughly 700–800 m lower, which is why its winters are milder and oranges ripen on the slopes around it.
intro: Takdah is for people who like old houses, slow mornings and walks without a ticket counter. There is no market street to speak of, no viewpoint queue and little to do except wander under the pines between bungalows, walk down into the tea, visit the orchid centre and climb the 3 km to Tinchuley for the view. Most visitors come for one night on a Lamahatta, Takdah and Tinchuley loop. We think two nights is better: one full day lets you walk to Rungli Rungliot and back, and gives the mist a chance to lift.

It is also one of the cheaper stays near Darjeeling. Homestays here, including some in the old cantonment bungalows, usually charge ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast. Getting here costs more than staying: shared jeeps are few, so most people hire a car from Darjeeling or come up from Teesta Bazar. Pack a torch and a warm layer even in April. Evenings are quiet, power cuts happen, and you should carry enough cash, because ATMs you can rely on are back in Darjeeling or Kalimpong.
facts: Jio and Airtel in most spots; patchy under the trees

highlights.title: The cantonment bungalows
highlights.text: Officers' bungalows from the early 1900s, with verandahs, fireplaces and tin roofs, scattered along the spur under tall pines. A few have been restored as heritage homestays; others you see from the lane. Walk them in the early morning, when the light comes low through the trees and the mist still lies in the valley.

highlights.title: Government orchid centre
highlights.text: A state orchid nursery with shade sheds of hill orchids, some of them native to these slopes. Flowering is best from February to April; in other months there is less colour, but it still makes a pleasant hour. Opening hours and fees vary, so ask at your homestay before you walk over.

highlights.title: Rungli Rungliot tea garden
highlights.text: The tea estate below Takdah, whose name the local story translates as 'thus far and no further'. Walk the garden roads between March and November, watch the pluckers at work in the morning, and ask at the office whether the factory takes visitors that day.

highlights.title: The walk to Tinchuley
highlights.text: Tinchuley is about 3 km up the road, an hour on foot. Go early for the Gumbadara viewpoint and Kanchenjunga, have tea in the village and walk back through orange orchards. You pass farmhouses, terraced fields and tea plots rather than shops, and the return is mostly downhill.

highlights.title: Gielle tea estate
highlights.text: Another garden close to Takdah, on the slopes toward the Teesta. Few visitors come this way, so the roads between the tea rows are quiet, and from the upper sections the valley opens out below you. It makes a good half-day walk from March to November.

highlights.title: Long evenings by the fire
highlights.text: Takdah goes quiet by 7 pm. Some bungalow homestays still use their fireplaces, others a heater, and dinner is the family's own food: rice, dal, squash, local greens, sometimes chicken curry. Bring a book; this is a place for an early night and an early walk.

how_to_reach.text: From Darjeeling the road runs via Ghoom and Jorebunglow onto the Peshok road, past Lamahatta, then branches off for Takdah: about 28 km and 1.5 hours, ₹1,800–2,500 one way. A car for the day taking in Lamahatta, Takdah and Tinchuley costs ₹2,500–4,000. From NJP or Bagdogra expect ₹3,500–4,500 one way and 3.5–4 hours.

A few shared jeeps run between Darjeeling and Takdah, with seats at roughly ₹100–150. Timings change and seats fill fast, so ask at Darjeeling's motor stand the day before. Otherwise take a jeep bound for Teesta Bazar or Kalimpong, get off at the Takdah turning and have your homestay send a car. Check current status before you travel.

From Siliguri you can also come up through Sevoke and the Teesta valley to Teesta Bazar, then climb via Peshok to Takdah, a drive about as long as the Darjeeling route. The Teesta valley road (NH10) has had long closures since the October 2023 flood: check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Takdah has no hotels in the usual sense. Most beds are in family homestays spread along the old cantonment spur, and a few of the restored officers' bungalows are run as heritage homestays with meals included. Rates usually run ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast; bungalow rooms cost a little more than village rooms. Tinchuley, 3 km away, has a larger cluster of village homestays with views, and Lamahatta has more a few kilometres back toward Darjeeling. We do not name single properties here because owners and standards change; ask for recent photos of the room, the bathroom and the heater before you pay an advance.
tips: Carry enough cash for your whole stay, since card machines are rare and reliable ATMs are in Darjeeling or Kalimpong.
Book a car for the return before you arrive, because shared jeeps out of Takdah are few and leave early.
Come between February and April if orchids are the point; outside those months the orchid centre is mostly green leaves.
Ask your homestay whether hot water comes from a geyser or a bucket, and whether rooms have a heater, especially from December to February.
Combine Takdah with Tinchuley and Lamahatta, but sleep in Takdah or Tinchuley instead of rushing all three as a day trip.

experiences.title: Heritage bungalow walk in old Takdah
experiences.summary: A slow morning walk through the lanes of the old British cantonment, past officers' bungalows from the early 1900s, tall pines and the tea slopes below. No ticket and no guide needed; just ask before you step into anyone's garden.
body: Takdah's history is in its houses. The British army set up a cantonment on this spur in the early 1900s, and the officers' bungalows that went up then were built in the hill style of the time, with wide verandahs, fireplaces, tall chimneys and tin roofs. They stand well apart, each in its own garden, along lanes that follow the contour of the hill. Walking between them shows you the shape of the old cantonment better than any map, and it costs nothing but a morning.

Start from your homestay around 7 am, when the mist sits in the valley and the light comes low through the pines. Follow the road along the spur, then take the smaller lanes that branch off between the houses. Some bungalows have been restored and run as homestays; others are lived in by families or are slowly decaying. Photograph from the lane, and if you want to see a verandah up close, ask. People here are used to visitors and will usually say yes or point you to a house that welcomes guests.

Allow two hours with stops. The lanes are not steep, but they are uneven, and wet leaves make them slippery in the monsoon, so good shoes matter more than fitness. Finish with tea at your homestay and ask the family what they know about their own house: who lived there, when it changed hands, which rooms are original. Stories vary from house to house, and we would rather you hear them from the people who live there than from us.

faqs.q: Can we go inside the old bungalows at Takdah?
faqs.a: Only those run as homestays, and usually only if you are staying there or ask politely first. The others are private homes. Walk the lanes, photograph from the road, and if a verandah catches your eye, ask whoever is there. Most families are friendly about it, but treat it as their home, not a museum.

faqs.q: Do we need a guide for the bungalow walk?
faqs.a: No. The lanes are short, safe and easy to follow, and your homestay can sketch a route in a minute. A local companion adds stories about who lived where, so if your host offers to walk with you, accept, and agree a small thank-you in advance; ₹200–500 is fair for a morning.

faqs.q: When is the best time of day for photographs?
faqs.a: Early morning, from about 6.30 to 8.30 am, between October and April. The low sun comes through the pines and lights the bungalow fronts, and mist often lies in the valley below. By late morning cloud usually builds, and afternoons in the monsoon are mostly grey and wet.

experiences.title: Orchid centre visit in flowering season
experiences.cost: Small fee or free · check locally
experiences.summary: An hour among the shade sheds of Takdah's government orchid centre, best from February to April when most of the hill orchids flower. Close to most homestays, cheap or free, and a good reason to time a Takdah trip for late winter.
body: The eastern Himalaya is orchid country, with several hundred species growing across Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills. On mossy trunks in the forests around Darjeeling, Kurseong and Kalimpong you find everything from tiny epiphytes with flowers the size of a rice grain to showy sprays of Dendrobium and Cymbidium. Takdah's government orchid centre is a nursery where some of these are grown under cover. It is not a show garden. It is a working place with shade sheds, potting benches and rows of plants, and that is part of its appeal.

Come between February and April, when most of the plants flower, and go in the late morning when the sheds are warm and the light is good. Staff are usually busy, but if you show interest someone may point out the plants that grow wild on these slopes. Hours and fees are set by the department and change, and the centre may be shut on holidays, so ask your homestay or check at the gate before you walk over. In the monsoon and early winter far less is in flower.

Keep the visit short and combine it with a walk through the cantonment lanes or down toward the tea; your homestay will tell you the best route from where you are staying. Do not pick or buy plants taken from the wild: many hill orchids are protected, and collecting them is illegal. If plants are offered for sale at the centre, ask whether they are nursery-grown, and remember that airlines and some states have rules on carrying live plants and soil.

faqs.q: When do the orchids flower at Takdah?
faqs.a: Most flowering is from February to April, with a few plants in bloom either side of that. Outside those months you will mostly see green leaves and the nursery at work. If orchids are the main reason for your trip, aim for March and ask your homestay a week ahead how the season is going.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee at the orchid centre?
faqs.a: If there is a fee it is small and set by the government department, and it changes, as do the opening hours. Ask your homestay or check at the gate before walking over. Carry small notes, because change can be hard to find, and expect it to be shut on some public holidays. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can we buy orchids to take home?
faqs.a: Only nursery-grown plants, and only if the centre is selling that day. Never buy orchids dug from the forest; many hill species are protected in India and collecting them is an offence. Check airline rules on live plants before you buy, since soil and pots are often a problem in baggage.

experiences.title: Down to Rungli Rungliot through the tea
experiences.cost: Free · factory visit only if allowed
experiences.summary: A half-day walk from Takdah down into the Rungli Rungliot tea garden, whose name the local story reads as 'thus far and no further'. Garden roads, workers' settlements, pluckers at work in season and, on a good day, a look inside the factory.
body: Darjeeling's tea gardens are not all on the Kurseong road. East of the town, on the long slopes falling toward the Teesta, gardens such as Rungli Rungliot and Gielle grow tea lower down than the famous estates around Darjeeling, and they see far fewer visitors. Rungli Rungliot lies below Takdah. Its name, the local story says, means 'thus far and no further', and the same name, spelt Rangli Rangliot, belongs to a community development block of the district. Ask in the village who first said those words; you may hear more than one version.

The walk follows the road and garden paths down from Takdah, through tea rows, shade trees and the small settlements where garden workers live. In the plucking season, from March to November, you will see teams of women working along the bushes with baskets on their backs, mostly in the morning. Keep to the roads and main paths, do not step into the rows, and ask before photographing anyone at work. If you want to see inside the factory, ask at the office; visits depend on the day's work and the manager's permission.

Allow three to four hours for the round trip, more if you stop for tea in a village shop. Going down is easy; coming back up is the real effort, so start early, before the sun gets strong. Carry water and a snack, wear shoes with grip and keep a rain jacket handy from June to September. If your legs are done at the bottom, a local car back up to Takdah usually costs a few hundred rupees; take a driver's number from your homestay before you set out.

faqs.q: Do we need permission to walk in the tea garden?
faqs.a: Walking on the roads and main paths through the garden is generally fine, and local people use them every day. Going into the tea rows, entering the factory or photographing workers up close needs permission. Ask at the garden office or through your homestay, be polite, and accept a no if the day is busy.

faqs.q: Is the Rungli Rungliot walk hard?
faqs.a: The way down is easy. The climb back to Takdah is steady and takes most people 1.5 to 2 hours, longer in heat or rain. Anyone used to walking an hour or two will manage at a slow pace. If you have bad knees or little time, walk down only and arrange a car to bring you back.

faqs.q: Can we buy tea from the garden?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Gardens occasionally sell packets at the factory, but there is no visitor shop with fixed hours, and stock varies with the season. Ask your homestay. If you want the garden's tea for certain, look for it in Darjeeling's tea shops and check the label for the garden name and the flush.

experiences.title: Walk the ridge road from Takdah to Tinchuley
experiences.summary: A 3 km climb from Takdah to Tinchuley through pines, orange orchards and village houses, timed to reach the Gumbadara viewpoint while Kanchenjunga is still clear. Tea in Tinchuley, then an easy walk back for breakfast.
body: Takdah and Tinchuley are neighbours, about 3 km apart, and the walk between them is the best way to understand both. Takdah sits lower among the cantonment bungalows and pines. Tinchuley sits higher, at about 1,770 m, a farming village of orange orchards, small tea plots and homestays, with a viewpoint at Gumbadara. The road climbs steadily between them, and on foot you notice what a car hides: the terraces, the cow sheds, children walking to school, prayer flags on bamboo poles.

Leave Takdah around 6 am in the clear months. Kanchenjunga is most often visible early, before cloud rises from the valleys, and the walk up takes about an hour at a steady pace. From Gumbadara the view runs north to the snow peaks and east down into the Teesta valley. Take a flask of tea or buy a cup in the village, and give yourself half an hour at the top. Even when the mountains hide, the valley and the light on the ridges are worth the climb.

Walk back the same way or, if you have arranged it, let a car collect you in Tinchuley. The road has light traffic, but jeeps come fast round the bends, so keep to the edge and walk in single file. Orange season, roughly November to January, is the prettiest time: fruit hangs over the walls and you may be offered some by the families who grow it. If they sell to you, pay what they ask; it will be cheap, and it is their income.

faqs.q: How long is the walk from Takdah to Tinchuley?
faqs.a: About 3 km each way by road, roughly an hour uphill and 45 minutes back at an easy pace. Add half an hour at the Gumbadara viewpoint and time for tea in the village, and the whole outing fits into a morning of about three hours.

faqs.q: Will we see Kanchenjunga on the walk?
faqs.a: On clear mornings from October to early December and in March and April, often yes, from Gumbadara and other open spots near Tinchuley. Cloud usually builds by 9 or 10 am, so go early. In the monsoon the mountains are hidden most days. No one can promise a view, so plan two mornings if it matters.

faqs.q: Is it safe to walk on the road?
faqs.a: Yes, with ordinary care. Traffic is light, but jeeps and cars take the bends fast, so walk single file on the edge, keep children close and avoid walking after dark. Wear something bright in mist, which can cut visibility to a few metres within minutes.

faqs.q: How far is Takdah from Darjeeling?
faqs.a: About 28 km by road, 1.5 hours by car via Ghoom, Jorebunglow and the Peshok road past Lamahatta. A reserved car costs ₹1,800–2,500 one way, or ₹2,500–4,000 for a full day covering Lamahatta, Takdah and Tinchuley. Shared jeeps are few; ask at Darjeeling's motor stand the day before.

faqs.q: Is Takdah worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want quiet, old houses and walks rather than sights. Takdah has British-era cantonment bungalows, an orchid centre, tea gardens below and the Tinchuley viewpoint 3 km away. It has no shops or nightlife to speak of. Families wanting busy days for children may prefer Darjeeling or Mirik; couples and walkers usually love it.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Takdah?
faqs.a: October to early December for clear views, and February to April for orchids and warmer days. December and January are cold at night but often sunny. June to September brings heavy rain, leeches on the paths and frequent mist, though prices drop and the tea is at its greenest.

faqs.q: Can we stay in a British-era bungalow in Takdah?
faqs.a: Yes. A few of the old cantonment officers' bungalows have been restored and run as heritage homestays, usually with meals included. Expect high ceilings, wooden floors, a fireplace or heater and simple bathrooms, at a little more than village homestay rates. Ask for recent photos before booking, because upkeep varies.

faqs.q: How much does a trip to Takdah cost?
faqs.a: Budget about ₹2,000–3,000 per person per day. Homestays cost ₹1,500–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast, and food extras are small. Transport is the bigger cost: a car from Darjeeling is ₹1,800–2,500 one way, or ₹3,500–4,500 from NJP or Bagdogra. Sharing a car between four brings it down sharply.

faqs.q: What is the difference between Takdah and Tinchuley?
faqs.a: Takdah is the old cantonment, lower down, with bungalows, pines, the orchid centre and tea gardens below. Tinchuley is a farming village 3 km higher up the ridge, with more homestays and the Gumbadara viewpoint for Kanchenjunga. They are close enough to stay in one and walk to the other.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network in Takdah?
faqs.a: Jio and Airtel usually work in most of the village, though signal drops under the trees and in some rooms. Data is enough for messages and maps, not for long video calls. Power cuts happen, so carry a charged power bank and a torch, especially in the monsoon.

faqs.q: Can we visit Takdah as a day trip from Darjeeling?
faqs.a: You can, as part of a car tour with Lamahatta and Tinchuley that takes six to eight hours and costs ₹2,500–4,000 for the car. You will see the place but miss its best part, the quiet morning and evening. We suggest at least one night if your plan allows.

faqs.q: Is Takdah good for older parents or small children?
faqs.a: Yes, for a calm stay. The drive is about 1.5 hours from Darjeeling, the walks are gentle and homestay food is simple and fresh. Medical facilities are limited, though, and the nearest hospitals are in Darjeeling and Kalimpong. Carry regular medicines and choose a room with an attached bathroom.
